provenance.method: lesson notes written from the NERDC 2025 scheme of work outline; every week keeps its scheme topic and bullets as the teaching spine

topics.title: Drama: text two
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify key events in each act of the second drama text.
The students should be able to compare and contrast themes between two drama texts.
Introduction:
We have previously studied the first drama text and now we will examine the second text. Comparing these texts will help us understand different dramatic approaches.
Content:
The second drama text will be studied act by act. Each act contains significant plot developments and character interactions. Students will identify the rising action, climax, and falling action in each act. We will compare the themes of power, love, and betrayal in both texts. For example, how does the portrayal of authority in the first text differ from the second? Students should note the dramatic techniques used by each playwright.
Class activity:
Students will work in groups to create a Venn diagram comparing the two drama texts, focusing on themes, characters, and settings.
Evaluation questions:
1. What is the main conflict in Act 2 of the second drama text?
2. How does the theme of power differ between the two drama texts?
3. Identify one dramatic technique used in the second text and explain its effect.
Summary:
Today we have explored the second drama text and compared it with the first, noting similarities and differences in themes and techniques.

topics.title: Drama: dramatic techniques
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to define irony and conflict in dramatic literature.
The students should be able to analyze how dramatic techniques create meaning in a text.
Introduction:
We have studied drama texts and now we will focus on the specific techniques playwrights use to engage audiences. Understanding these techniques is essential for exam success.
Content:
Dramatic techniques include irony, conflict, foreshadowing, and symbolism. Irony occurs when there is a discrepancy between appearance and reality. For example, a character boasting about their honesty while stealing. Conflict drives the plot forward and can be internal or external. Students will analyze examples of irony and conflict in the drama texts. We will practice essay writing by structuring arguments around how these techniques develop themes.
Class activity:
Students will select a scene from the drama text and identify examples of irony and conflict, then write a paragraph explaining their effects.
Evaluation questions:
1. Define dramatic irony with an example from the texts studied.
2. How does conflict contribute to the development of the main character?
3. Write an introduction for an essay discussing the use of irony in the drama text.
Summary:
Today we have examined dramatic techniques focusing on irony and conflict and practiced analyzing their effects in drama texts.

topics.title: Prose: themes
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify major themes in the prose text.
The students should be able to write an essay analyzing themes in the prose text.
Introduction:
After studying drama, we now turn to prose literature. Themes are central to understanding any literary work and form a significant part of the Literature exam.
Content:
The prose text contains several important themes including love, tradition versus modernity, and social justice. Students will identify how these themes are developed through characters, plot, and setting. For example, how does the protagonist's journey reflect the theme of tradition versus modernity? We will discuss the moral lessons embedded in these themes. Students will practice writing structured essays that analyze how themes are developed and their significance in the text.
Class activity:
Students will work in pairs to identify three major themes and find textual evidence for each, then present their findings to the class.
Evaluation questions:
1. What is the main theme in the prose text?
2. How does the setting contribute to the development of themes?
3. Write a body paragraph analyzing how the theme of love is developed in the text.
Summary:
Today we have identified and analyzed the major themes in the prose text, practicing how to write effective essays on this topic.

topics.title: Prose: setting and plot
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to explain how setting influences the plot in the prose text.
The students should be able to answer structure-based questions on the prose text.
Introduction:
We have examined themes in the prose text and now we will focus on how setting and plot work together to create meaning. Understanding these elements is crucial for answering prose questions in exams.
Content:
The setting of the prose text includes both time and place, which significantly influence the characters' actions and the plot's development. Students will analyze how the historical period and geographical location affect the story's events. The plot structure follows a clear pattern of exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, and resolution. We will practice answering structure-based questions that require analyzing how plot elements are connected. Students will learn to identify key turning points in the narrative.
Class activity:
Students will create a plot diagram of the prose text, identifying the main events and explaining how the setting influences each stage.
Evaluation questions:
1. How does the setting influence the protagonist's decisions?
2. Identify the climax of the prose text and explain its significance.
3. Write an answer to a structure-based question analyzing the relationship between setting and plot.
Summary:
Today we have explored how setting and plot interact in the prose text, practicing answering structure-based exam questions.

topics.title: Poetry: new poems
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to analyze the content and structure of unseen poems.
The students should be able to identify poetic devices in unseen poems.
Introduction:
We have previously studied known poems and now we will develop skills for reading and analyzing unseen poems. This is an essential skill for the Literature exam.
Content:
Reading unseen poems requires careful attention to content, structure, and language. Students will practice identifying the speaker, situation, and theme in unfamiliar poems. We will analyze poetic devices such as imagery, metaphor, and symbolism in the new poems. For example, how does the poet use imagery to create a vivid picture of the harmattan season? Students will learn to approach poems methodically, first understanding the literal meaning before exploring deeper interpretations.
Class activity:
Students will work in groups to analyze a new poem, identifying its theme, structure, and poetic devices, then present their analysis to the class.
Evaluation questions:
1. What is the main theme of the unseen poem?
2. Identify two poetic devices used in the poem and explain their effects.
3. How does the structure of the poem contribute to its meaning?
Summary:
Today we have practiced the skills needed to analyze unseen poems, focusing on content, structure, and poetic devices.

topics.title: Poetry: comparison
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to compare two poems based on theme, structure, and language.
The students should be able to write a comparative essay on two poems.
Introduction:
After analyzing individual poems, we will now develop skills for comparing two poems. Comparison is a key requirement in the Literature exam and tests deeper understanding.
Content:
When comparing two poems, students should consider similarities and differences in theme, structure, and language. For example, how do two poems about nature differ in their use of imagery? We will examine how poets use different techniques to explore similar themes. Students will practice writing comparative essays that analyze both poems and make meaningful connections between them. The essay should have a clear structure with introduction, body paragraphs comparing specific aspects, and conclusion.
Class activity:
Students will select two poems and create a comparison table, noting similarities and differences in theme, structure, and language, then use this to plan an essay.
Evaluation questions:
1. What theme is common to both poems compared in class?
2. How does the structure of the first poem differ from the second?
3. Write an introduction for a comparative essay on the two poems studied.
Summary:
Today we have practiced comparing two poems based on theme, structure, and language, and planned comparative essays.

topics.title: Context questions
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to quote accurately from literary texts.
The students should be able to explain the significance of quoted passages in context.
Introduction:
Context questions form an important part of the Literature exam and require precise knowledge of texts and ability to explain passages in their proper context.
Content:
Context questions require students to quote accurately from literary texts and explain the significance of quoted passages. Students will practice identifying relevant quotes that support specific points. For example, when asked about a character's motivation, students should find and quote the exact dialogue or narration that reveals this. We will practice explaining quotes by considering their position in the text, their relationship to themes, and their effect on the reader. Students will learn to provide detailed explanations that go beyond literal interpretation.
Class activity:
Students will work in pairs to create context questions for each other based on the drama and prose texts, then exchange and answer them.
Evaluation questions:
1. Quote a passage that reveals the protagonist's attitude toward tradition.
2. Explain the significance of the following quote in its context: [quote from text].
3. How does the quoted passage contribute to the development of theme?
Summary:
Today we have practiced the skills needed to answer context questions, focusing on accurate quoting and detailed explanation.

topics.title: Character analysis
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to differentiate between main and minor characters in literary texts.
The students should be able to write an essay analyzing a character's development.
Introduction:
Characters are central to literature and understanding their motivations and development is essential for literary analysis. We will focus on both main and minor characters in the texts studied.
Content:
Main characters are central to the plot and undergo significant development, while minor characters often serve to highlight aspects of main characters or advance the plot. Students will analyze how characters are developed through dialogue, action, and description. For example, how does the protagonist's relationship with a minor character reveal important traits? We will practice writing character analysis essays that examine motivations, relationships, and development. Students should use textual evidence to support their analysis.
Class activity:
Students will select either a main or minor character and create a character profile, analyzing their traits, relationships, and significance in the text.
Evaluation questions:
1. What is the role of the minor character in advancing the plot?
2. How does the protagonist change throughout the text?
3. Write a body paragraph analyzing a character's motivation.
Summary:
Today we have analyzed both main and minor characters, practicing how to write effective character analysis essays.

topics.title: Mock paper one
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to complete a Literature exam paper under timed conditions.
The students should be able to evaluate their own performance and identify areas for improvement.
Introduction:
After studying various literary elements, we will now apply this knowledge by completing a mock exam paper. This will help prepare students for the actual WAEC examination.
Content:
Students will complete Paper One of the mock Literature exam under timed conditions. The paper will include questions on drama, prose, and poetry, testing various skills including analysis, comparison, and context interpretation. After completion, we will mark the papers using the WAEC marking scheme. Students will identify their strengths and weaknesses in different question types. For example, students may find context questions challenging but excel at theme analysis. We will discuss strategies for improving performance in weaker areas.
Class activity:
Students will exchange papers and mark them according to the WAEC marking scheme, then discuss common errors and effective approaches.
Evaluation questions:
1. Which question type did you find most challenging in the mock exam?
2. What strategies will you use to improve your performance in the Literature exam?
3. Identify one area where you performed well and explain why.
Summary:
Today we have completed a mock exam paper and evaluated our performance, identifying areas for improvement before the actual WAEC examination.

topics.title: Revision and WAEC practice
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to apply exam techniques to past WAEC questions.
The students should be able to identify common patterns in WAEC Literature questions.
Introduction:
As we approach the final weeks before the exam, we will focus on revision and practicing past WAEC questions to build confidence and familiarity with the exam format.
Content:
We will work through past WAEC Paper Two questions on drama, prose, and poetry. Students will practice structuring answers according to the marking scheme. We will identify common question patterns and effective approaches for different question types. For example, how to approach a comparative essay or a context question. Students will learn to manage their time effectively during the exam and prioritize questions based on their strengths. We will review key literary terms and concepts that frequently appear in the exam.
Class activity:
Students will work in groups to answer a past WAEC question, then present their answer to the class for feedback.
Evaluation questions:
1. What is the most common question type in past WAEC Literature papers?
2. How should you structure a comparative essay in the exam?
3. Identify one literary term that frequently appears in WAEC questions and explain its importance.
Summary:
Today we have practiced past WAEC questions and reviewed exam techniques to prepare for the upcoming examination.
